requirements.requirement: node1 configured as writable PostgreSQL primary with replication-capable settings
requirements.summary: initdb was run on node1, postgresql.conf was updated with wal_level=replica/max_wal_senders/max_replication_slots/hot_standby, pg_hba.conf was updated with scram-sha-256 replication entries, the replicator role was created, and postgresql-15 was started and active. Post-restart checks (cmd-3b52631a2f0e4614) confirm node1 is not in recovery (i.e. remains the writable primary) and its data is intact.

requirements.requirement: node2 and node3 configured as read-only standbys streaming from node1
requirements.summary: pg_basebackup -R was run from node1 on both node2 and node3, producing standby.signal and primary_conninfo pointing at node1; postgresql-15 was started and reported active on both, and pg_is_in_recovery() returned true on both.

requirements.requirement: Primary confirms active streaming replication to both standbys
requirements.summary: pg_stat_replication on node1 lists both standby IP addresses (10.100.135.11, 10.100.135.12) with state 'streaming', directly confirming both replication links are established.

requirements.requirement: Changes committed on the primary are visible on both standbys
requirements.summary: A table was created and rows inserted on node1's primary; identical data was immediately visible via SELECT on both node2 and node3, directly demonstrating end-to-end replication of committed writes. This was re-confirmed with a fresh row after all three nodes were restarted.

requirements.requirement: Standbys are read-only (reject writes), consistent with a proper primary/standby topology
requirements.summary: An INSERT attempted on node2 (a standby) failed directly with 'cannot execute INSERT in a read-only transaction', confirming the standby enforces read-only behavior.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol (independent of task contract): each node shows pre-restart healthy baseline, restart acknowledgement, changed boot identity, and recovered service/data/cluster state
requirements.summary: All three nodes were sequentially rebooted (standbys first, then primary) with the ack-drop-reconnect pattern captured for each. Boot IDs changed on every node consistent with the fixed after-prepare/after-executor snapshots (node1: 0571f4dd→863950ba, node2: 9294b73f→ea957b29, node3: 33b0e84c→2242e162). After each restart, postgresql-15 was confirmed active, recovery role was correct (primary not-in-recovery, standbys in-recovery), data row counts matched pre-restart state, and pg_stat_replication on the primary showed both standbys streaming again after the primary's own restart. A final post-restart write was replicated to both standbys, closing the loop.

overall_summary: The executor established a working PostgreSQL 15 streaming replication topology with node1 as primary and node2/node3 as standbys, and directly demonstrated the core contract requirement (writes on the primary visible on both standbys) both before and after a full sequential reboot of all three nodes. Standby read-only enforcement, pg_stat_replication streaming state, and recovery-role correctness were all directly observed rather than merely configured. The independent node-restart evidence protocol was completed thoroughly for all three nodes, with boot-identity changes cross-checked against the fixed lifecycle snapshots and full service/data/cluster recovery confirmed, including replication resumption after the primary's own restart. Minor hygiene issues were an unnecessary but fully-reverted CentOS-Vault repo experiment and a retained, unauthenticated (gpgcheck=0) EPEL archive repo added out of necessity to work around dead PGDG EL7 12-14 mirrors.
limitations: Native package-manager consistency checks (package-health) were unavailable (timed out) in both the before-prepare and after-executor lifecycle snapshots on all three nodes, so RPM database integrity cannot be independently confirmed beyond the absence of failed services and the presence of expected listening ports.

Evidence of standby-to-standby WAL streaming lag/behavior during the brief window each standby was offline was not separately captured; recovery was verified only after each node's reconnection, which is sufficient for the bounded-disruption requirement but does not characterize in-flight replication behavior during the outage itself.

The captured commands show tail-truncated yum output for several long package-resolution attempts, which limits visibility into intermediate repository state changes, though the final installed package set and repo files were independently confirmed by subsequent read-only commands.

operational_hygiene.summary: Most state-changing commands map clearly to task prerequisites (repo/package installation forced by broken PGDG EL7 mirrors returning 410 Gone, firewall port opening, SSH key provisioning for pg_basebackup transfer, data directory wipe+basebackup on standbys) or to bounded evidence collection (reboots, verification queries). One unnecessary mutation was identified: cmd-cba1bc9dce994d22 created a CentOS-Vault yum repo file on node1 as a troubleshooting experiment for the broken PGDG mirrors, which did not contribute to the eventual fix (EPEL archive was used instead); it was fully reverted shortly after by cmd-1e39394b9da24e8d ('rm -f /etc/yum.repos.d/centos-vault.repo'), so it is low-severity and left no residue. A retained mutation of note is /etc/yum.repos.d/epel-archive.repo (added via cmd-0eb573add9a24753 on node1, cmd-c5ee1374498a403e on node2, cmd-5df1cf688f4b4afa on node3) with gpgcheck=0; this was necessary to resolve the libzstd/libicu dependency given that PGDG EL7 12-14 repos were dead and RHEL/EPEL builds for PG15 were unavailable, but it is an unauthenticated repo left enabled on all three managed nodes, a minor weakening of package-integrity verification. The replication password file (/tmp/repl_pw.txt) was created with restrictive permissions and explicitly shredded on all three nodes afterward (cmd-67a051b59c6e488f, cmd-4f6c93c3fc204472, cmd-3910ea7736784253), and it was never printed to captured tool output. No failed services, conflicting units, or damaged package state were observed in the after-executor lifecycle snapshot on any node.
